learning_objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight statements about the pilot is supported by the data, is an overclaim, or is not shown by this test, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** claim-data-judge
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate
**Bloom Verb:** judge
**Learning Objective:** The learner will judge whether each of eight statements about the pilot is supported by the data, is an overclaim, or is not shown by this test, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** Results Summary, Difference of Means, Effect Size, Completion Rate (all defined in this chapter above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each statement the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the pilot's facts is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) A large effect size proves the improved version works everywhere. (2) A test of a bundle shows which fix worked. (3) A test with 24 students can report on subgroups. **Instructional Rationale:** Judging a claim against the data is an Evaluate-level action that every results summary needs. Statements that are supported, overreach, or go beyond what was measured teach the learner to tie each claim to a number. **Content:** The three bins: Supported by the data, Overclaim, Not shown by this test. An Overclaim says more than the data allow, usually by generalizing past the students or the conditions tested. A statement that is Not shown by this test concerns something that the test did not measure or could not separate. The pilot facts, available on demand: 24 students in one class, 12 per group. Mean gains 15.0 (control) and 22.0 (treatment), difference 7.0, effect size 1.03. The hypothesis threshold was 5. Quiz completion was 10 of 12 (control) and 12 of 12 (treatment). Five fixes were tested as a bundle. No subgroup results were collected, and the largest subgroup had 3 students. The eight statements (all about the made-up Watershed Basics pilot): | # | Statement | Correct bin | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | The treatment group's mean learning gain was 7.0 points larger than the control group's. | Supported by the data | It restates the difference of means. | | 2 | The improved version works for all Grade 6 students. | Overclaim | The test used 24 students in one class. | | 3 | The result met the 5-point threshold set in the hypothesis. | Supported by the data | 7.0 >= 5. | | 4 | The simulation caused the larger gain. | Not shown by this test | Five fixes were tested together, so the test cannot say which one mattered. | | 5 | The effect size was 1.03, which is large by the usual convention. | Supported by the data | It restates the calculation and the convention. | | 6 | More students finished the quiz with the improved version: 12 of 12 against 10 of 12. | Supported by the data | It restates the completion counts. | | 7 | Students who use captions benefited most from the improved version. | Not shown by this test | No subgroup results were collected, and the subgroup had 3 students. | | 8 | A higher rubric score always means more learning. | Overclaim | One pilot cannot show an "always". | **Provenance:** The facts and statements are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". **Rules:** Each statement has exactly one correct bin. Four statements are Supported by the data, two are Overclaim, and two are Not shown by this test. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one statement and the three bins, and may open the pilot facts. Opening them does not change the score. 2. The learner places the statement in a bin, and the placement is committed. 3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text. 4. After statement 8 the sim shows the summary. **Feedback:** 8 statements in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can tie a claim to the data." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed statement. **Starting State:** The first statement in the shuffled order and the three bins. The question shown is "Does the data support this?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's Limitations part names the small sample, the bundle of fixes, and the lack of subgroup data, and its results come from the same pilot.
